items.title: 68357_Jimmy Maxwell oral history interview
items.q: As Wingy Manone once said, it never got over the Rocky Mountains.

ctx.x: It was difficult, living in the San Joaquin Valley. The other kids in town were interested in music but not to the extent I was. And not having any money, this is the Depression

years, my father was out of work for several of those years. There wasn't that much jazz coming out to California anyhow. As Wingy Manone once said, it never got over the Rocky Mountains. But about once a month one Armstrong record would come out and one Duke Ellington record would come out. And some way I would beg, borrow or even steal, truthfully, for one of these records. And I started copying off -- also tried to copy off the Duke Ellington records.

I didn't know anything about harmony or anything but I knew the names of triads. So if I had what I guess you would call a C ninth, that -- a C 13th. I remember "Blue Ramble" is the first tune I copied and the chord -- and I had a C, A, E, G, D, B flat, see, in the bass. So I called that a G minor chord and A minor chord with C in the bass.
